chapters.title: Jeremiah is called and strengthened

parts.text: Jeremiah’s ministry is introduced from Josiah’s reign to Jerusalem’s captivity. The LORD tells him that he knew and appointed him as a prophet before birth. Jeremiah objects that he is young, but God commands him to speak whatever he is sent to say and promises deliverance. Touching his mouth, the LORD gives him words to uproot and overthrow, and to build and plant.

An almond branch confirms God’s readiness to perform his word, and a boiling pot signals judgment coming from the north upon Judah’s idolatry. Jeremiah must not be intimidated. Though rulers, priests, and people oppose him, God makes him like a fortified city and promises to be with him.

chapters.title: Israel abandons the fountain of living waters

parts.text: The LORD remembers Israel’s early devotion and asks what fault her ancestors found in him. Priests, rulers, and prophets have all turned away. Unlike nations that retain their false gods, Israel exchanged her glory for what cannot profit. The offence is pictured as forsaking living water to dig broken cisterns. Foreign alliances cannot repair the consequences of abandoning the LORD.

Israel denies defilement despite persistent idolatry and is compared to an unrestrained creature pursuing lovers. Like a thief caught in the act, the nation is exposed, yet turns to God only in trouble. Its many gods cannot save. Innocent blood, refusal of correction, and changing political refuges reveal continuing rebellion and bring shame instead of security.

chapters.title: Return, faithless Israel

parts.text: The LORD compares Israel’s idolatry to marital unfaithfulness. Judah saw her sister’s rejection and exile, yet repeated the same conduct and returned only outwardly. Withholding rain did not bring shame or sincere repentance. God judges treacherous Judah as less excusable because she witnessed Israel’s example.

Nevertheless, Israel is invited to acknowledge iniquity and return to the merciful LORD. He promises faithful shepherds, gathering to Zion, and a time when Jerusalem is called his throne and nations gather there. Judah and Israel will return together. The chapter closes with an answering confession of shame, failed reliance on the hills, and salvation found only in the LORD.

chapters.title: A warning from the north and a vision of desolation

parts.text: Israel is urged to return sincerely, remove abominations, and practice inward rather than merely outward consecration. Trumpets announce destruction from the north, and a lionlike destroyer approaches. Jerusalem must wash wickedness from its heart, because its own ways have brought bitterness. Kings, priests, and prophets are shaken by the prospect of siege.

Jeremiah cries out in anguish at the sound of war. He sees earth without form and void, darkened heavens, trembling mountains, absent people and birds, and ruined cities beneath the LORD’s anger. Yet God says he will not make a full end. Jerusalem’s attempts to attract former lovers cannot prevent their hostility, and Zion cries like a woman in travail.

chapters.title: Corruption from the streets to the leaders

parts.text: A search for someone practicing justice and truth exposes Jerusalem’s refusal to receive correction. Poor and great alike have broken the yoke. Adultery, idolatry, and denial of God’s warnings lead to an approaching nation whose language is unknown and whose forces consume the land’s resources. Yet the LORD will not make a full end. Foreign service answers their former service to strange gods.

The people fail to fear the One who sets the sea’s boundary and supplies seasonal rain. Their sins withhold good things, while wealthy deceivers trap others and neglect the fatherless and needy. Prophets speak falsely, priests rule through corrupt means, and the people welcome it. The final question asks what they will do when its consequences arrive.

chapters.title: Rejected warnings and an advancing siege

parts.text: Benjamin is warned to flee Jerusalem as a northern enemy prepares siege. The city overflows with oppression, violence, and injustice, and the LORD urges correction before desolation. Jeremiah’s hearers cannot bear the word, while all ranks pursue dishonest gain. Leaders offer shallow healing and proclaim peace when there is no peace, without even blushing at wrongdoing.

The LORD calls the people to the old good paths and appoints watchmen, but they refuse both instruction and alarm. Imported incense cannot replace obedience. A cruel army approaches, producing fear and mourning. Jeremiah’s task is compared to testing metal, but the refining exposes persistent corruption; the people are called rejected silver because the LORD rejects them.

chapters.title: The temple cannot shelter persistent rebellion

parts.text: Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and calls Judah to amend its conduct. The temple’s presence is no guarantee of safety while oppression, innocent bloodshed, idolatry, theft, and adultery continue. Treating worship as permission for wrongdoing turns God’s house into a den of robbers. Shiloh’s earlier fate warns that this sanctuary too can be abandoned and the people cast out.

The LORD forbids intercession for a people whose households unite in serving other gods. Obedience, not sacrifice detached from listening, was the heart of his command, yet successive generations rejected the prophets. Child sacrifice at Tophet will bring the place a new identity as a valley of slaughter. Joy and wedding songs will cease in the desolated land.

chapters.title: False peace and the grief of an unhealed people

parts.text: Judgment will expose the bones of Judah’s leaders and people before the heavenly bodies they worshiped. The living remnant will prefer death. Unlike migrating birds that know their seasons, the people refuse to recognize the LORD’s judgment or repent. Their claim to wisdom fails because they reject his word, while prophets and priests heal superficially and announce nonexistent peace.

The coming enemy brings trembling, and the people seek fortified places without finding safety. They acknowledge sin yet face approaching destruction and uncharmable serpents. The prophet grieves over a people who cry for help after the harvest and summer have passed without salvation. His questions about balm and a physician in Gilead express anguish at their continuing wound.

chapters.title: Weeping over deceit and boasting only in the LORD

parts.text: Jeremiah longs for tears enough to mourn his slain people and for a refuge from their treachery. Lies have made even neighbours and relatives unsafe, and refusing to know the LORD has become habitual. God will refine and judge them. The land’s desolation is explained by rejection of his law and pursuit of Baal, bringing bitter affliction and scattering among unknown nations.

Mourning women are summoned as death enters homes and the young are cut off. Wisdom, strength, and wealth provide no ground for boasting. The proper boast is knowing the LORD, who delights in lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness. Judgment will reach both outwardly circumcised and uncircumcised peoples, for Israel’s heart remains uncircumcised.

chapters.title: Lifeless idols and the living Creator

parts.text: Israel must not learn the nations’ fears or worship objects fashioned from wood and decorated with precious metal. Such idols must be carried and cannot act. The LORD is the living God and everlasting king, incomparable in wisdom and power. He made the earth, established the heavens, and governs rain and wind. Jacob’s portion is the Maker of all things, not a craftsman’s image.

The people are told to prepare for removal from the land. A lament describes a ruined tent, scattered children, and shepherds who failed to seek the LORD. A northern invasion approaches. The speaker acknowledges that people cannot direct their own steps and asks correction in judgment rather than annihilating anger, while appealing for judgment upon nations that devour Jacob.

chapters.title: The broken covenant and a plot against Jeremiah

parts.text: Jeremiah is told to proclaim the covenant that required obedience when God brought Israel from Egypt. The people repeatedly followed their own stubborn hearts and returned to their ancestors’ idolatry. Disaster is therefore coming, and their many gods cannot answer. The LORD again forbids intercession and describes the once-flourishing olive tree as marked for burning because of its evil.

God reveals a plot against Jeremiah, who had been like a lamb unaware of the slaughter being planned. He entrusts his cause to the righteous judge. The men of Anathoth have threatened death if he continues prophesying in the LORD’s name, so God announces judgment upon them and their households in the appointed time.

chapters.title: Jeremiah questions the prosperity of the treacherous

parts.text: Acknowledging God’s righteousness, Jeremiah asks why treacherous people prosper while keeping God near their lips and far from their hearts. He asks that God distinguish his own inward loyalty from theirs. The answer challenges him to prepare for harder trials: if running with footmen wearies him, how will he contend with horses? Even relatives may speak pleasantly while betraying him.

The LORD laments the abandonment and ravaging of his beloved inheritance, devastated by destructive shepherds and armies. Yet judgment upon Judah’s harmful neighbours is not the final word: after uprooting them, God promises compassion and return to their lands. If they learn his people’s ways and swear by his name, they will be established among his people. Nations that refuse obedience, however, will be uprooted and destroyed.

chapters.title: The ruined girdle and Judah’s pride

parts.text: Jeremiah wears a linen girdle, then hides it by the Euphrates as commanded. When recovered, it is ruined and useless. The LORD explains that Judah’s pride will likewise be marred: the people were meant to cling to him for praise and glory but refused to hear. A second image portrays all ranks filled with drunken confusion and dashed against one another.

The prophet urges humility before darkness falls and warns the king and queen of coming humiliation. Judah will be carried away, its trusted associates turning into masters. Deeply ingrained evil is compared to the difficulty of changing skin or a leopard’s spots. Jerusalem’s exposed shame follows forgotten allegiance and idolatrous unfaithfulness, leaving the question of cleansing urgently open.

chapters.title: Drought, false promises, and a plea for mercy

parts.text: Severe drought empties water supplies, cracks the ground, and leaves people and animals desperate. A prayer confesses sin and asks the LORD not to act like a stranger or helpless man. Yet God refuses to overlook the people’s wandering. Prophets promising peace without sword or famine were never sent by him; both they and those who trust them will face the very disasters they deny.

Jeremiah is instructed to lament the grievous wound of his people. Sword outside and famine within expose the catastrophe. The prayer again acknowledges ancestral and present wickedness, asking God not to dishonour his glorious throne or break his covenant. Only the LORD can send rain, so the people wait upon him.

chapters.title: Jeremiah’s anguish and renewed commission

parts.text: The LORD says that even the intercession of Moses and Samuel would not reverse the announced judgment. Death, sword, famine, and captivity await, and Judah’s fate is associated with the evil done under Manasseh. Repeated rebellion has exhausted the previous pattern of relenting, and bereavement and widowhood will multiply across the land.

Jeremiah laments the conflict surrounding his ministry, recalls delighting in God’s words, and asks why his wound remains incurable. The LORD calls him to return and distinguish the precious from the worthless so he may continue as his mouth. Jeremiah must not conform to his opponents. God promises to make him a fortified wall and rescue him from their power.

chapters.title: Signs of coming grief and a greater return

parts.text: Jeremiah is forbidden to marry, raise children, join mourning houses, or share feasts, because death, abandoned bodies, and the end of ordinary joy are approaching. When the people ask why, he must explain that their own stubbornness has exceeded their ancestors’ idolatry. They will be expelled to an unfamiliar land where they serve other gods.

A future restoration will be so notable that return from the northern land and other countries becomes a new testimony alongside the exodus. Before that, God’s searching judgment reaches hidden places and repays pollution of his land. Nations will eventually acknowledge the emptiness of inherited idols, and the LORD will make his power and name known.

chapters.title: The searching LORD and the sabbath test

parts.text: Judah’s sin is engraved deeply in heart and altar, bringing loss of inheritance. Trust in human strength is compared to a barren shrub; trust in the LORD to a tree beside water. God searches the deceitful heart and repays conduct. Jeremiah prays for healing and rescue, refuses the charge that he desired calamity, and asks vindication against persecutors.

At Jerusalem’s gates, Jeremiah commands observance of the sabbath: no burdens are to be carried through the city, and work must cease as commanded to the fathers. Obedience is linked with continuing royal life and worship in Jerusalem. Refusal will bring an unquenched fire upon its gates and palaces.

chapters.title: The potter’s lesson and opposition to the prophet

parts.text: At the potter’s house, Jeremiah watches a marred vessel reshaped into another. The LORD applies the image to his authority over nations: announced destruction may be withheld if they turn from evil, while promised good may be withdrawn if they disobey. Judah is therefore urged to abandon its evil plans, but replies that it will follow its own stubborn heart.

The LORD expresses astonishment that his people have forgotten him and left ancient paths for stumbling roads, making their land a desolation. Opponents then plan to discredit Jeremiah while trusting existing priests, counsellors, and prophets. He recalls having interceded for them and asks God to judge the murderous plot rather than overlook their wickedness.

chapters.title: A broken bottle announces irreversible ruin

parts.text: Jeremiah takes a potter’s bottle and elders to the valley of Hinnom. He announces disaster because Judah has forsaken the LORD, filled the place with innocent blood, and burned children to Baal, acts God never commanded. The valley will be renamed for slaughter. Siege will bring appalling hunger, even the eating of children and neighbours.

Jeremiah breaks the bottle before the witnesses, declaring that the people and city will be broken like pottery that cannot be restored. Burial will extend into Tophet, and houses defiled by rooftop worship will share its uncleanness. Returning to the temple court, he announces the same disaster because the people have hardened themselves against God’s words.

chapters.title: Pashur’s punishment and Jeremiah’s inner struggle

parts.text: Pashur the priest strikes Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks. After release, Jeremiah gives him a new name meaning surrounding terror and announces that he and his household will be taken to Babylon. Judah’s strength, treasures, and kingly possessions will also fall into enemy hands. Pashur will die there with those misled by his false prophecies.

Jeremiah describes the ridicule his message brings and the inward fire that prevents him from remaining silent. He hears threats even from familiar companions, yet confesses the LORD’s power to defend him and calls for praise. The chapter then turns sharply into anguish, as he curses the day of his birth and asks why he was born to sorrow.

chapters.title: Life through surrender rather than false security

parts.text: Zedekiah sends officials to ask whether the LORD will perform a wonder against Babylon’s siege. Jeremiah answers that God will turn Judah’s own weapons against it and fight the city in anger. Pestilence, sword, and famine will leave survivors for Nebuchadrezzar’s hand. The people are given a stark choice: remaining in the city leads to death, while surrendering to the Chaldeans preserves life.

The royal house is commanded to execute justice and deliver the oppressed, lest wrath burn beyond remedy. Jerusalem’s confidence in its position and defences cannot prevent judgment. The LORD will repay the fruit of its deeds and consume the surrounding strength on which it relies.

chapters.title: Judgment upon Judah’s kings

parts.text: The royal house is commanded to uphold justice, rescue the oppressed, and stop violence against strangers, orphans, and widows. Obedience would preserve royal passage through the gates, but refusal will reduce the house to desolation. Nations will recognize that abandonment of the covenant caused the ruin. The people should mourn especially for Shallum, who has gone into captivity and will not return.

Jehoiakim is condemned for building luxurious houses through unpaid labour, unlike Josiah’s care for the poor. He faces a dishonourable burial. Coniah is compared to a signet God will remove, carried with his mother into exile. Though he has descendants, none will prosper by ruling on David’s throne in Judah.

chapters.title: Faithful shepherding and the exposure of false prophets

parts.text: The LORD condemns shepherds who scatter and destroy his flock. He will gather the remnant and appoint shepherds who care for them. A righteous Branch raised to David will reign wisely, securing Judah and Israel, and will be called THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS. The future gathering becomes a defining act of deliverance alongside the exodus.

Jeremiah grieves over corrupt prophets and priests who strengthen evildoers and promise peace without God’s commission. True speakers of God’s counsel would turn people from wickedness. Dreams and borrowed words cannot replace the LORD’s word, which is compared to fire and a hammer. Misusing the claim of a divine burden brings reproach and judgment instead of authority.

chapters.title: Two baskets of figs distinguish two futures

parts.text: After Jeconiah and many skilled people are carried to Babylon, Jeremiah sees two baskets before the temple: one contains excellent figs, the other fruit too bad to eat. The good figs represent the exiles whom the LORD regards for good. He will restore and establish them, giving them a heart to know him so they return wholeheartedly and become his people.

The bad figs represent Zedekiah, his officials, and the remaining people in Jerusalem and Egypt. They will become a reproach and curse among the nations. Sword, famine, and pestilence will pursue them until they are consumed from the land, overturning any assumption that avoiding the first exile guaranteed safety.

chapters.title: Seventy years and the cup for the nations

parts.text: Jeremiah recalls twenty-three years of rejected warnings. Because Judah would not listen or abandon idols, the LORD will bring Nebuchadrezzar against the land and its neighbours, silencing ordinary joy and making them serve Babylon for seventy years. When those years end, Babylon itself will be punished for its iniquity, and its deeds repaid.

Jeremiah is then given the cup of divine wrath to present to nations, beginning with Jerusalem and extending through surrounding kingdoms and distant peoples. No nation can refuse judgment when the city bearing God’s name is already being judged. The LORD’s worldwide controversy is pictured through storm, sword, fallen multitudes, and the terrified cries of rulers whose pastures are devastated.

chapters.title: Jeremiah is tried for warning of the temple’s fall

parts.text: At the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, Jeremiah speaks in the temple court, offering the possibility that repentance may avert disaster. If the people refuse the law and prophets, the house will become like Shiloh. Priests and prophets seize him and demand death. Before the officials, Jeremiah insists the LORD sent him, urges amendment of conduct, and warns that killing him will bring innocent blood upon them.

Officials and elders defend him, recalling how Micah warned Hezekiah without being executed and how repentance brought mercy. A contrasting account tells of Urijah, who fled to Egypt but was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim. Ahikam’s support protects Jeremiah from the crowd.

chapters.title: The yoke of Babylon must be accepted

parts.text: The LORD directs Jeremiah to make yokes and send a message to neighbouring kings through their envoys in Jerusalem. As Creator, God has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar for an appointed period. Nations that submit may remain in their lands; those refusing will face sword, famine, and pestilence. Prophets, dreamers, and diviners promising escape from Babylon’s rule are misleading their hearers.

Jeremiah gives the same counsel to Zedekiah, priests, and people: serve Babylon and live. Claims that the temple vessels will soon return are false. Instead, the remaining vessels will also go to Babylon and stay until the LORD’s appointed visitation, when he will restore them.

chapters.title: Hananiah breaks the yoke and receives judgment

parts.text: Hananiah publicly announces that the LORD has broken Babylon’s yoke and will return the temple vessels and exiles within two years. Jeremiah wishes such restoration were true but notes that a prophet promising peace is shown to be sent by the LORD when the prediction is fulfilled. Hananiah then breaks the wooden yoke from Jeremiah’s neck and repeats his promise of imminent freedom.

After Jeremiah withdraws, the LORD sends him back with a contrary message: the broken wooden yokes will be replaced by iron, and the nations will continue serving Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah tells Hananiah that God did not send him and that his false assurance teaches rebellion. Hananiah will die that year, and he dies in its seventh month.

chapters.title: A letter teaches the exiles how to live in Babylon

parts.text: Jeremiah writes to the exiles, telling them to build homes, plant gardens, marry, raise families, and seek the peace of the city where God has sent them. Its welfare affects their own. They must reject prophets promising a different timetable. After seventy years at Babylon, the LORD will fulfil his good word, hear wholehearted seekers, and gather them back with a future of peace and hope.

The letter warns that those remaining under Jerusalem’s king face judgment, and names false prophets whose adultery and lies bring punishment. Shemaiah has written demanding Jeremiah’s restraint for advising a long stay. God declares that Shemaiah and his descendants will not share the promised good because he taught rebellion without divine commission.

chapters.title: Jacob’s trouble and promised restoration

parts.text: Jeremiah is commanded to write God’s words of restoration for Israel and Judah. A uniquely dreadful time of Jacob’s trouble is described, yet Jacob will be saved out of it. The foreign yoke will be broken, and the people will serve the LORD and David their king, whom God raises for them. They need not fear ultimate extinction, though correction will not be withheld.

Their wound is incurable by ordinary help, and former lovers have abandoned them because of accumulated sin. Nevertheless, the LORD will heal, restore homes and worship, multiply the people, and raise a ruler from among them. They will be his people and he their God. His anger will accomplish its purpose, understood more fully in the latter days.

chapters.title: Israel gathered and a new covenant promised

parts.text: The LORD promises to rebuild Israel in everlasting love. The scattered return with weeping and guidance, including the blind, lame, and mothers, and find abundance and renewed joy. Rahel’s lament is answered with hope for her children’s return. Ephraim’s repentance meets fatherly compassion. Judah’s towns and fields will again receive blessing, and the weary will be refreshed.

God promises to plant where he once uprooted and to judge each person’s own iniquity. He will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the broken covenant of the exodus: his law will be written within them, all will know him, and sins will be remembered no more. The enduring order of creation guarantees Israel’s continuing place before him, and Jerusalem will be rebuilt as holy ground.

chapters.title: A field purchase witnesses to future restoration

parts.text: While Jerusalem is besieged and Jeremiah is confined for predicting its capture, his cousin Hanameel offers him a field at Anathoth. Recognizing God’s word, Jeremiah buys it for seventeen shekels of silver, seals the deed, and has witnesses confirm it. He directs Baruch to preserve the documents in an earthen vessel because houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in the land.

Jeremiah prays, acknowledging God’s creation, justice, exodus deliverance, and the people’s disobedience, yet asks about buying land amid certain defeat. God answers that nothing is too hard for him. Jerusalem must fall for its persistent wickedness, but he will gather the people, make an everlasting covenant, and restore secure life and ordinary purchases.

chapters.title: Restoration and the enduring promises to David

parts.text: Still confined, Jeremiah receives a further invitation to call upon the LORD and hear great things. Though the city is filled with destruction, God promises healing, return, rebuilding, and cleansing from sin. Jerusalem will become a source of joy and honour before nations. Wedding songs, thanksgiving offerings, and flocks counted by shepherds will return to its desolated places.

The LORD promises a righteous Branch for David, bringing judgment, salvation, and security. David’s royal line and the Levitical priestly service are upheld by a promise compared with the established covenant of day and night. As the heavenly host cannot be numbered, their increase cannot be measured. God rejects the claim that he has finally cast away his chosen people.

chapters.title: A broken emancipation covenant brings judgment

parts.text: As Babylon attacks Jerusalem and the remaining fortified cities, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that the city will burn and he will be captured and meet Babylon’s king. Yet Zedekiah will not die by the sword; his death will be accompanied by mourning like that given to former kings. Jeremiah delivers this message while Lachish and Azekah still stand.

The people had made a covenant to free their Hebrew servants, then forced them back into bondage. The LORD condemns this reversal as a violation of his name and of the law requiring release. Because they refused true liberty, he announces their release to sword, pestilence, and famine. Babylon’s temporarily withdrawn army will return, capture, and burn the city.

chapters.title: The Rechabites’ obedience exposes Judah’s refusal

parts.text: Jeremiah brings the Rechabites into a temple chamber and offers them wine. They refuse because their ancestor Jonadab commanded them not to drink, build permanent houses, sow fields, or plant vineyards, but to live in tents. They have obeyed through generations and are only in Jerusalem because the invading armies made residence outside dangerous.

The LORD uses their conduct as a contrast with Judah. These people honour an ancestor’s instruction, while Judah refuses God’s repeated words through the prophets. Disaster therefore follows the nation’s refusal to listen and turn from evil. The Rechabites, however, receive a promise that Jonadab’s family will not lack someone to stand before the LORD.

chapters.title: Jehoiakim burns the scroll, but the word remains

parts.text: The LORD tells Jeremiah to record his warnings in a scroll so Judah may hear, repent, and receive forgiveness. Baruch writes Jeremiah’s dictated words and reads them publicly at the temple during a fast. Officials summon him, hear the scroll in fear, and decide the king must know. They advise Baruch and Jeremiah to hide before reporting it.

As the scroll is read to Jehoiakim, he cuts and burns it piece by piece despite pleas to stop. He orders the writers arrested, but the LORD hides them. God commands another scroll, announces judgment upon the king and his line, and has Baruch write the former words again, with many additional warnings.

chapters.title: Jeremiah is arrested during a pause in the siege

parts.text: Zedekiah, his servants, and the people do not obey the LORD, yet the king asks Jeremiah to pray. Pharaoh’s approaching army temporarily causes the Chaldeans to withdraw. God warns that Egypt will return home and Babylon will renew the attack and burn Jerusalem. Even wounded Chaldean survivors would accomplish the judgment; the pause is no assurance of rescue.

As Jeremiah leaves toward Benjamin, a guard accuses him of deserting to Babylon. Despite his denial, officials beat and imprison him. Zedekiah later consults him secretly and again hears that he will be delivered to Babylon. At Jeremiah’s request, the king transfers him from the dungeon to the court of the prison and provides bread while supplies last.

chapters.title: Rescue from the dungeon and a final warning to Zedekiah

parts.text: Officials accuse Jeremiah of weakening resistance by telling the people that surrender preserves life. With Zedekiah’s permission, they lower him into the dungeon, where there is no water but mire, and he sinks. Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian official, appeals to the king against the injustice. Authorized to rescue him, he uses ropes and worn cloths to lift Jeremiah safely, after which the prophet remains in the prison court.

Zedekiah privately seeks another word, and Jeremiah again promises survival if he surrenders. Refusal will bring burning, capture, and humiliation of the royal household. The king fears surrendered Judeans but receives assurance if he obeys. He orders secrecy about the conversation, and Jeremiah remains confined until Jerusalem falls.

chapters.title: Jerusalem falls and God’s servants are preserved

parts.text: After a prolonged siege, Babylon breaches Jerusalem. Zedekiah and his soldiers flee by night but are overtaken near Jericho. At Riblah, his sons and Judah’s nobles are killed before him; he is then blinded, bound, and taken to Babylon. The royal house and other houses are burned, walls broken, and survivors deported. Poor people left in the land receive fields and vineyards.

Nebuchadrezzar commands that Jeremiah be treated well, and officials release him into Gedaliah’s care. The chapter also records God’s earlier promise to Ebed-melech: the city’s threatened disaster will come, but he will escape the sword and keep his life because he trusted the LORD.

chapters.title: Gedaliah gathers the remnant but dismisses a warning

parts.text: Released from chains at Ramah, Jeremiah hears Babylon’s captain acknowledge that the LORD’s judgment came because Judah disobeyed. He is offered a choice of going to Babylon under protection or staying wherever he wishes. Jeremiah returns to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lives among the remaining people.

Judean military leaders and refugees from neighbouring lands gather around Gedaliah, whom Babylon has appointed governor. He encourages them to serve Babylon peacefully, settle in the towns, and gather the harvest. Johanan warns that Ammon’s king has sent Ishmael to assassinate Gedaliah and secretly offers to prevent it. Gedaliah refuses to believe the accusation and forbids action against Ishmael.

chapters.title: Gedaliah is murdered and the remnant flees

parts.text: Ishmael and ten men share a meal with Gedaliah, then kill him, the Judeans with him, and the Chaldean soldiers present. He also deceives a group of mourning travellers and murders most of them, sparing ten who reveal hidden supplies. The bodies are cast into a pit. He captures the remaining people of Mizpah and sets out toward Ammon.

Johanan and other commanders pursue Ishmael and meet him near Gibeon. The captives rejoice at the rescue and join Johanan, while Ishmael escapes with eight men. The rescued group stops near Beth-lehem on the way toward Egypt, fearing Babylonian retaliation because Ishmael killed its appointed governor.

chapters.title: The remnant asks for guidance but is warned against Egypt

parts.text: The remaining people and their commanders ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD’s direction, promising obedience whether the answer pleases them or not. After ten days, the word comes: they should remain in the land. God will build and plant them rather than destroy them and will show mercy so Babylon’s king also treats them mercifully.

If they instead choose Egypt to escape war, alarm, and hunger, those very dangers will follow them. Sword, famine, and pestilence will consume those determined to settle there. Jeremiah reminds them of their pledge and exposes the dishonesty of requesting guidance they do not intend to follow. The place they desire as refuge will become their place of death.

chapters.title: The people enter Egypt against God’s word

parts.text: Azariah, Johanan, and other proud leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying and claim that Baruch has influenced him to deliver them to Babylon. Rejecting the LORD’s command to remain, they take the remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt. They arrive at Tahpanhes, carrying their disobedience into the refuge they had chosen.

There the LORD tells Jeremiah to hide large stones in the clay at Pharaoh’s palace entrance before witnesses. God declares that Nebuchadrezzar will set his throne over that place and bring destruction to Egypt. Death, captivity, and sword await its people; its temples and images will be burned or broken. Egypt will not provide safety from Babylon’s reach.

chapters.title: Idolatry continues among the refugees in Egypt

parts.text: Jeremiah addresses the Jews living throughout Egypt, reminding them that Jerusalem’s ruin followed idolatry and refusal of repeated prophetic warnings. They are now provoking the same anger through worship in Egypt, threatening to cut off their own remnant. The LORD announces sword and famine, with only a few escaping to the land to which they hope to return.

The people openly refuse his message and insist that offerings to the queen of heaven formerly brought prosperity. Jeremiah replies that those practices caused Judah’s destruction rather than preventing it. God declares that his word, not theirs, will stand. Pharaoh-hophra’s delivery into enemy hands will serve as a sign of the judgment overtaking their chosen refuge.

chapters.title: Baruch receives a promise of preservation

parts.text: A brief message returns to the time when Baruch wrote Jeremiah’s words during Jehoiakim’s fourth year. Baruch has lamented that the LORD added grief to sorrow and that weariness has left him without rest. God answers that he is breaking down what he built and uprooting what he planted throughout the land. Baruch should therefore not seek great things for himself amid such judgment. Yet the LORD promises a personal mercy: wherever Baruch goes, his life will be preserved as his portion of escape.

chapters.title: Egypt’s defeat and Israel’s continuing hope

parts.text: An oracle concerning Egypt describes Pharaoh-necho’s army at Carchemish, defeated by Nebuchadrezzar. Military preparation and confident boasting cannot prevent panic and retreat. Egypt rises like a flood intending conquest, but the day belongs to the Lord GOD of hosts as a day of vengeance. Its wounded strength cannot be healed by gathering remedies, and its shame is heard among nations.

A further warning announces Babylon’s coming attack upon Egypt itself. Hired soldiers and mighty men fall because the LORD drives them away, and Egypt’s gods, rulers, and supporters face punishment. Nevertheless, afterward the land will again be inhabited. Jacob is separately reassured of eventual return and measured correction rather than complete destruction.

chapters.title: The sword appointed against the Philistines

parts.text: Before Pharaoh strikes Gaza, the LORD gives Jeremiah a warning against the Philistines. A northern invasion is pictured as waters flooding cities and land. The noise of horses and chariots creates such panic that fathers cannot turn back for their children. Philistine strength and the helpers of Tyrus and Zidon are cut off. Gaza mourns, and Ashkelon is silenced. A plea asks the LORD’s sword to rest, but it cannot be still while carrying out his appointed charge against the coast.

chapters.title: Moab’s pride is broken, yet restoration is promised

parts.text: Moab’s cities face devastation because the nation trusted its works and treasures. Chemosh goes into captivity with priests and rulers. Long security is compared to wine left undisturbed in its vessel, but the vessels will now be emptied and broken. Moab’s shame over Chemosh mirrors Israel’s shame over Beth-el. Judgment spreads across its towns, breaking the horn and arm of its strength.

Pride against the LORD and mockery of Israel bring humiliation. The prophet mourns ruined vineyards, lost wealth, and silenced harvest joy while disaster sweeps through the land. Escape from one danger only leads to another. Yet the oracle closes with the LORD’s promise to restore Moab’s captivity in the latter days.

chapters.title: Judgments upon Ammon, Edom, and other nations

parts.text: Ammon is judged for occupying Gad’s territory and trusting its riches, though a later return is promised. Edom’s vaunted wisdom and mountain strongholds cannot protect it. God uncovers its hiding places, brings loss upon its households, and declares a desolation comparable to Sodom and Gomorrah. Its pride is exposed, and a powerful enemy descends like a lion and eagle.

Damascus loses courage and faces burning palaces. Kedar and Hazor are warned to flee Nebuchadrezzar, whose forces will seize their flocks and possessions. Elam’s military strength is broken and its people scattered in every direction as God establishes judgment over it. Nevertheless, the LORD promises to bring Elam’s captivity back in the latter days.

chapters.title: Babylon falls and Israel seeks the LORD

parts.text: Babylon’s fall is proclaimed along with the shame of its gods. A northern enemy makes the land desolate, while Israel and Judah return weeping, seeking the LORD and an everlasting covenant. The people are urged to leave Babylon. Because it plundered God’s inheritance and rejoiced in oppression, the same violence returns upon it. Israel’s scattering is remembered, but the LORD promises restoration and pardon for the remnant.

Babylon is trapped because it contended against the LORD. Armies are summoned to repay its deeds and avenge his temple. Israel’s redeemer is strong and will plead the people’s cause. Sword, drought, and ruin strike Babylon’s rulers, defenders, and wealth, and the earth trembles at the report of its capture.

chapters.title: Babylon’s recompense and the sinking scroll

parts.text: The LORD announces Babylon’s destruction and urges his people to flee before sharing its punishment. Once a golden cup making nations drunk, Babylon falls suddenly. God’s creative power is contrasted with lifeless idols, and armies are summoned, including the kings of the Medes, to fulfil judgment. Babylon’s violence against Zion and its destructive power will be repaid; even its defences cannot prevent invasion.

The city is likened to a threshing floor ready for harvest. The LORD answers Zion’s complaint, dries Babylon’s waters, humiliates Bel, and brings lasting ruin upon rulers and walls. Jeremiah gives Seraiah a scroll containing these judgments to read in Babylon. He must then tie it to a stone and throw it into the Euphrates, portraying Babylon’s sinking without recovery.

chapters.title: The fall of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin’s release

parts.text: The final account recounts Zedekiah’s evil reign and rebellion against Babylon. Siege brings famine and a breach in Jerusalem’s defences. Zedekiah flees, is captured near Jericho, witnesses the execution of his sons and officials, and is blinded and imprisoned in Babylon. Nebuzar-adan burns the temple, palace, and houses, demolishes the walls, and deports survivors while leaving some poor people to cultivate the land.

Temple furnishings and metals are removed, captured officials are executed, and the numbers taken in successive deportations are recorded. The book closes years later with Evil-merodach releasing Jehoiachin from prison, speaking kindly to him, giving him honoured standing, and providing a daily allowance and regular place at the royal table.
